title: AI-enabled business models in legal services: from traditional law firms to next-generation law companies?
pub: Journal of Professions and Organization, vol. 7, no. 1, pp. 27–46
author: John Armour · Mari Sako

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Big Four: Integration matters more than replacement
st.an: The source accepts convergence around integrated, multidisciplinary delivery rather than straightforward Big Four replacement of law firms. It materially extends the proposition by explaining how AI scale economics, acquisitions, complementary expertise and partnership governance shape integration, and by predicting value capture by both new entrants and diversified incumbent firms.
qs: Some of these firms will be new entrants; others will  be incumbent law firms that diversify so as simultaneously to pursue legal advisory and one or  more of the new AI-enabled business models.

Legal human capital will also be required in these firms (or parts of them) that  pursue the new business models, but in a way that interfaces closely with other components of  a multidisciplinary team.

st.t: Competitive strategy: Build-versus-buy becomes a portfolio
st.an: The source accepts that sourcing is not a binary choice and materially extends the proposition with a three-part organisational framework: advisory specialisation, contracting across multiple providers, and vertical integration. It also develops the portfolio logic by identifying platform-dependence risks and shared ownership or joint ventures as intermediate governance options.
qs: This has led many firms to diversify by establishing tentative relationships with multiple  providers.

(c) Combining the legal advisory with new business models through vertical integration     Other law firms have sought to combine their existing legal advisory business model with  new AI-enabled business models through vertical integration.

st.t: Law-firm pyramid: Efficiency threatens revenue and training
st.an: The source accepts that AI selectively automates junior production while retaining complementary human work, and materially extends the cluster by explaining how business models, scalability and multidisciplinary organization determine structural change and who captures the resulting value. It strengthens the cluster’s buyer-and-business-model account, though it does not directly develop the apprenticeship concern.
qs: In particular, we highlight the central importance of business  models and organizational complements in mediating how AI affects the complex interplay of  task substitution, task augmentation, and the creation of new tasks.

Moreover, step IV (generate outputs) no longer requires a large number  of junior associates and paralegals doing document reviews for example, but rather is  automated using machines supported by a modest number of staff.

st.t: Legal economics: AI makes adoption a model problem
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s central proposition that AI adoption is an organizational and business-model problem rather than a technology purchase. It materially develops that view by identifying partnership-governance constraints and concrete organizational responses—including contracting, equity stakes, joint ventures and separate corporate subsidiaries—and by explaining how these structures affect value capture among law firms, clients, ALSPs, vendors and incumbents.
qs: Major law firms as  partnerships have wrestled with implementing AI and related technologies due to the absence  of complements to AI-enabled business models; first, relevant non-legal human capital inside  the firm, and second, a governance structure that does not constrain risk-taking and exclude  people with essential technological and other expertise from the firm’s decision-making  process.

In such cases, differences in organizational structure and human  capital mix mean that merging the subsidiary into the legal advisory business model is neither  feasible or desirable; rather the firm seeks to pursue different business models at the parent  (partnership) and subsidiary (company) levels.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s task-level, human-complementary account of AI and materially extends it by specifying how business models, multidisciplinary assets, organizational governance and capital shape deployment and value capture. It gives less attention to verification and apprenticeship risks, but does not conflict with them.
qs: In particular, we highlight the central importance of business  models and organizational complements in mediating how AI affects the complex interplay of  task substitution, task augmentation, and the creation of new tasks.
Thus, the introduction of  AI substitutes for humans in step IV (generate outputs), but humans complement the AI  system’s design and application in all other steps.

st.t: Operating model: AI shifts bargaining across providers
st.an: The source accepts that AI is reshaping legal-service operating models and bargaining across corporate clients, law firms, legal operations providers, technology providers and the Big Four. It materially extends the cluster by explaining value capture through contracting, client bypass, multidisciplinary capabilities and renegotiation risks, while retaining a role for lawyer-led advisory partnerships.
qs: On  the one hand, where legal operations or technology providers are also seeking to market  directly to corporate clients, the law firm may be concerned that clients will ultimately bypass  them in these aspects of the work.

Second, while corporate clients themselves may capture some of the value created by  AI’s application to legal services, this will likely be shared with firms that adopt new business  models for the provision of legal services.

st.t: Partnership structure: AI tests governance beyond capital scarcity
st.an: The source accepts that partnerships remain effective for reputation-intensive legal advice while arguing that AI-enabled legal operations and technology expose governance, investment-horizon and multidisciplinary-career constraints. It materially develops the cluster by linking business models to organizational forms and mapping adaptation through contracting, subsidiaries, acquisitions and corporate-parent hybrids, subject to ownership regulation.
qs: This account of complementarities between business models, human capital, and  organizational forms has a clear implication: professional partnerships likely face internal  obstacles to the adoption of the legal operations and legal technology business models within  their existing organizations.

These conflicts are avoided in the first, partially externalized via contracting in the  second, and segregated and realigned by organizational restructuring in the third, type of  experimentation we outlined above.

st.t: Professional power: AI redistributes tasks and status
st.an: Armour and Sako strongly accept the cluster’s core proposition that AI redistributes legal tasks and professional roles through organisational choices rather than technical capability alone. They materially develop it by specifying how business-model complements, governance forms and multidisciplinary expertise shape substitution, augmentation, new tasks and emerging professional identities, while leaving organisational outcomes conditional.
qs: In particular, we highlight the central importance of business  models and organizational complements in mediating how AI affects the complex interplay of  task substitution, task augmentation, and the creation of new tasks.

Either way, the diffusion of multidisciplinary teams                    Electronic copy available at: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3418810 ^Lis likely to lead to the emergence of ‘hybrid professionals’ (who develop a relational capability  vis-à-vis expertise in other areas) or ‘organizing professionals’ (who embed organizing  capabilities with professional action) (Blomgren & Waks, 2015; Noordegraaf, 2007, 2015).

st.t: Task substitution: Complementarity can still reshape staffing
st.an: The source accepts the central proposition that AI can substitute for output-generation tasks while preserving complementary roles for lawyers. It materially develops that proposition through a workflow-stage account: staffing reductions are concentrated in scalable output production, while lawyers shift toward system design, oversight, review and client interpretation, often within multidisciplinary teams.
qs: Thus, the introduction of  AI substitutes for humans in step IV (generate outputs), but humans complement the AI  system’s design and application in all other steps.

Lawyers remain necessary for the successful  implementation of AI in legal services, but changes in work design resulting from AI adoption  are likely to alter the nature of lawyers’ job, not least by shifting the boundaries of  ‘jurisdictional domains’ to which lawyers make exclusive claims (Abbott, 1988).

st.t: Value capture: Integrated delivery reshapes market boundaries
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core proposition that AI-created value depends on integrated expertise, technology, workflows and organizational design rather than task efficiency alone. It materially develops that proposition by linking distinct delivery models to pricing, capital, governance and multidisciplinary capabilities, and by forecasting shared value capture among corporate clients, new entrants and diversifying incumbent firms while leaving viable combinations unsettled.
qs: Second, while corporate clients themselves may capture some of the value created by  AI’s application to legal services, this will likely be shared with firms that adopt new business  models for the provision of legal services.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts selective, task-level substitution rather than wholesale lawyer replacement and materially extends the cluster by specifying how business models, organizational complements, governance structures and multidisciplinary assets mediate deployment and value capture.
qs: In particular, we highlight the central importance of business  models and organizational complements in mediating how AI affects the complex interplay of  task substitution, task augmentation, and the creation of new tasks.

In short, we suggest that (a) some legal tasks will  remain beyond the capabilities of AI for the foreseeable future, and continue to be exclusively  performed by lawyers; (b) a few tasks will be substituted for by AI systems; and (c) that new  tasks are created in order to deliver AI systems, and these tasks that augment AI are carried out  by multidisciplinary teams of lawyers and other experts working together.

st.t: Workflow unbundling: Buyers challenge time-based production
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core account of disaggregated legal workflows, differentiated pricing and continued lawyer-led advice, then materially extends it with a task–business model–organization framework. It explains how capital, multidisciplinary skills, governance and organizational separation determine which providers can scale AI-enabled operations, while treating incumbent displacement as uncertain rather than inevitable.
qs: Third, we analyse the organizational structure that complements the old and new business models: the professional partnership (P2) is well- adapted to delivering the legal advisory business model, but the centralized management, access to outside capital and employee incentives offered by the corporate form appear better to complement the new AI-enabled business models.

st.t: Justice access: Direct AI use shifts risk downward
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s task-specific, human-supervised model: it distinguishes automatable tasks from work requiring human input and retains human involvement throughout implementation and review. It does not directly assess unrepresented users, remedies or verification risk, so its support is limited to the cluster’s workflow and augmentation claims.
qs: This workflow can then be reviewed to identify which tasks AI can replace  (that is, substitute for) and which tasks it will continue to require human input (that is, augment  the use of AI).
Of these, all steps except IV (generate outputs) require human inputs.

kp.k: Business models mediate AI's impact on legal work
kp.d: This theoretical paper, dated December 2019 and published in 2020, links tasks, business models and organizational structures, drawing on existing literature and emerging sector practices rather than presenting a new quantitative impact study. Armour and Sako argue that complementary assets and organizational arrangements shape task substitution, augmentation and creation; their conclusions about the profession's future are explicitly tentative.
qs: We develop our argument by transitioning through three levels of analysis: tasks, business models, and organizations.
We draw three tentative conclusions.
AI adoption is not just about technological innovation; it is fundamentally also about business model innovation with profound implications for the nature of the legal profession.

kp.k: Automation targets tasks rather than entire lawyer jobs
kp.d: The authors distinguish tasks remaining exclusively human, tasks substituted by AI and new tasks supporting AI delivery. Their account of contemporary supervised machine learning predicts continued human advantage in client interaction and genuinely novel, bespoke problem-solving because these require social or creative intelligence. These are time-qualified capability judgments, not claims about all future AI.
qs: A key point is that it is tasks that are automated, not jobs (Autor, 2015).
Where jobs contain a mix of some tasks that can be automated and some that cannot, human roles become more focused on those that cannot be automated.
So, for work that is exclusively ‘bespoke’—that is, novel in character and unlikely to be repeated—AI is unlikely to substitute for humans any time soon.

kp.k: Data and fixed costs determine scalable AI adoption
kp.d: The authors identify representative training data and expensive professional labelling as major constraints. They argue that AI's low prediction costs and potential increasing returns favour repeatable work and organizations with sufficient resources and volume. Citing ABA 2019 and LSB 2018, they report adoption concentrated in large organizations and predict corporate rather than consumer legal services will drive uptake.
qs: Second, labelling the training data for legal services generally requires expensive professional expertise.
As a result, there are high fixed costs to training a ML model.
This implies that corporate legal services rather than consumer legal services will drive the adoption of AI.

kp.k: AI workflows retain extensive multidisciplinary human work
kp.d: Their six-step workflow comprises problem definition, model selection and testing, data preparation, output generation, consistency review, and evaluation and explanation of implications. Only output generation is treated as automated. Lawyers supply legal knowledge, labelling, interpretation and client explanation; data scientists, engineers, security specialists, designers and project managers provide other essential inputs. Consistency review remains a human task distinct from evaluating and explaining implications.
qs: Of these, all steps except IV (generate outputs) require human inputs.

Moreover, these inputs are a combination of professional knowledge across different fields including law but also in data science, software engineering, information security, project management, and design thinking.
Thus, the introduction of AI substitutes for humans in step IV (generate outputs), but humans complement the AI system’s design and application in all other steps.

kp.k: Document automation reduces execution staffing, not all legal expertise
kp.d: In the proposed workflow, automated output generation replaces large numbers of junior associates and paralegals doing document review with machines and modest staffing. Lawyers remain necessary, but scalable applications concentrate their contributions in data labelling, oversight, interpretation and client interaction. The paper supplies no numerical displacement estimate.
qs: Moreover, step IV (generate outputs) no longer requires a large number of junior associates and paralegals doing document reviews for example, but rather is automated using machines supported by a modest number of staff.
lawyers remain necessary in the workflows, but their expertise is more focused on labelling legal data points and interpreting results to interface with human clients.

kp.k: Traditional advisory economics depend on lawyer leverage and reputation
kp.d: The traditional legal advisory ideal type sells bespoke advice through billable hours, captures value through trust and reputation, and measures profit per equity partner. Leverage means the associate-to-partner ratio: increasing it pushes work to the most junior capable lawyer. The authors argue that partnership governance complements this lawyer-human-capital model.
qs: Value creation to raise revenue is via the billable hour, an input-based approach to pricing
Value capture, measured by profit per equity partner, can also be improved by increasing the ratio of associates to partners, known as ‘leverage’.
Increasing leverage is achieved by pushing work down to the most junior person capable of doing it

kp.k: Three AI-enabled models have distinct assets and pricing
kp.d: The authors identify three ideal types. Their broadly defined 'legal operations' delivery model sells process efficiency using fixed or per-unit fees and combines data, systems and multidisciplinary expertise; it encompasses provider delivery as well as in-house processes. Legal technology vendors sell or license software, including SaaS, capturing value through intellectual property and platforms. Consulting designs and optimizes processes and technology implementation; because it is bespoke and human-capital-intensive, it typically retains hourly pricing, trust, reputation and leverage.
qs: The use of AI to predict pricing also enables the services to be sold for a fixed (or per-unit) fee, rather than on an hourly basis.
Value creation is based on product sales (licensing) or usage (so-called ‘software as a service’).
Because this work is human-capital intensive and bespoke, value creation is typically based on billable hours—input-based pricing.

kp.k: Partnership strengths can become barriers to organizational change
kp.d: The authors explain partnership's fit with advisory work through senior-lawyer ownership, cross-monitoring, homogeneous professional training, decentralized autonomy and promotion incentives. Those same complementarities make radical change difficult: consensus becomes costlier with heterogeneous expertise, while non-lawyers lack equivalent participation and rewards. Switching one practice without its complements may reduce performance.
qs: They are incentivized by contingent compensation in the form of meeting billable hour targets, and through promotion to partner as a reward
However, consensus-based governance and the distributed nature of authority among partners make the achievement of radical change and innovation particularly challenging
Moreover, profit-sharing between lawyers in a PSF is incompatible with recognizing contributions by non-lawyers.

kp.k: Corporate governance better complements technology-intensive service models
kp.d: The authors argue that legal operations and legal technology generally fit corporate organization better than traditional partnership because they require upfront risk capital, multidisciplinary teams and coordinated decisions. Outside shareholders, transferable equity, hierarchical management and stock incentives address partnership funding and incentive constraints. The fit is less clear-cut for bespoke consulting; the authors also acknowledge the Big Four's multidisciplinary partnerships as an exception to predominantly corporate new entrants.
qs: These aspects of the corporate form appear much more compatible with the emerging legal operations and legal technology business models than does the partnership form.
They also require investment of risk capital, to establish and organize technical systems in advance of associated revenues.
Matters are less clear-cut for the consulting business model

While the Big Four are not organized as companies, their multidisciplinary partnership structure is likely more amenable to the assembly of multidisciplinary teams than is a standard law firm partnership.

kp.k: Partner investment horizons constrain funding for innovation
kp.d: The proposed mechanism is that partners finance investment from retained profits or borrowing but receive profits only during their tenure, discouraging investments whose returns arrive after retirement. Borrowing is not a complete remedy because creditors are generally more conservative about project risk than equity investors. Corporate shareholders can instead sell shares reflecting expected future profits.
qs: Capital must either be sourced from partners’ accumulated profits or take the form of borrowing.

Partners only receive profits for the period of their tenure; as a result, they will only be willing to reinvest these (as opposed to paying them out) where returns will be generated prior to their retirement
Borrowing capital for investment is not a complete solution, as creditors are typically more conservative as regards project risk than equity investors

kp.k: In-house adoption faces investment and data obstacles
kp.d: Corporate clients possess governance, capital access and multidisciplinary employment structures conducive to adoption; GE, Barclays and BT illustrate restructuring efforts. Nevertheless, the authors argue that legal departments' cost-centre status makes investment harder to justify than revenue-generating projects. Fragmented legacy systems, insufficient data and insufficient volume further constrain internal deployment, potentially preserving demand for external providers able to aggregate work and data with clients' permission.
qs: They are viewed internally as a cost center, rather than a source of revenue.
An initial aspect is simply gaining access to internal data, which often will be spread across a multitude of legacy systems.
In contrast, legal services providers might have the potential to scale analysis of data provided by many clients, provided of course that clients are amenable to sharing data.

kp.k: New entrants combine delivery, software and consulting differently
kp.d: The paper distinguishes software vendors from legal-work providers. Technology startups assemble specialist teams and external investment but lack reputation and training data; established information providers such as LexisNexis and Thomson Reuters have data advantages. Law companies including UnitedLex, Elevate and Axiom pursue delivery models, sometimes combining technology and consulting. The Big Four seek integrated professional services; EY's Riverview Law acquisition in September 2018 and Pangea3 acquisition in April 2019 illustrate the authors' account.
qs: What start-ups lack, however, is reputation with users and access to data necessary to train AI models developed on their platforms.
These firms already have access to vast quantities of data, meaning that it will be much easier for them to scale AI that utilizes such data.
Second, the legal operations business model is being pursued by a group of rapidly-growing ‘law companies’ such as UnitedLex, Elevate, and Axiom.

kp.k: Law firms face three broad strategic responses
kp.d: The authors classify incumbent responses along a continuum: retain an exclusively advisory model; contract with technology and delivery providers; or vertically integrate new models. Advisory specialization preserves partnership's fit but relinquishes influence over how clients bundle other services and limits associated consulting opportunities. Contracting externalizes some organizational conflicts; integration segregates and realigns them.
qs: The three patterns in law firm adaptation to, and experimentation with, new AI-enabled business models can be understood as points on a continuum of engagement.

These conflicts are avoided in the first, partially externalized via contracting in the second, and segregated and realigned by organizational restructuring in the third, type of experimentation we outlined above.

kp.k: Contracting enables experimentation but creates dependency risks
kp.d: Contracts and incubators let firms test uncertain technologies without raising external financing or assembling complete multidisciplinary teams. The authors predict possible instability from providers selling directly to clients, renegotiating surplus allocation, and locking in platform-specific training benefits. Data pooling could strengthen provider market power. Equity stakes and joint ventures, illustrated by Slaughter and May's Luminance stake and Taylor Vinters' ThoughtRiver stake, may mitigate hold-up and adjustment costs.
qs: Such relationships enable the law firm to experiment with the utility of the provider’s products or services
Another problem is that contracting leaves open for renegotiation the division of the surplus generated by AI technology, as between the law firms and the providers.
increasing returns to scale may enable the provider to build market power.

kp.k: Subsidiaries separate conflicting models but retain funding constraints
kp.d: The paper describes captive service centres, internal technology teams and consulting units as forms of integration. Distinct cost or profit centres and corporate subsidiaries can give multidisciplinary units autonomy and reduce clashes with partnership incentives. However, parent-funded subsidiaries still lack outside capital. Their eventual trajectory is uncertain: scale may favour outside customers and spin-outs, while continued integration may catalyse reform of the parent firm.
qs: This parent-subsidiary structure minimizes negative synergies between the business models, and enables greater risk-taking within the subsidiary.
But to the extent that funds for investment come from the parent law firm, the subsidiary does not have access to external capital.
The long-term relationship between these new subsidiaries and their parent law firm is as yet unclear.

kp.k: DWF illustrates corporate ownership above a law partnership
kp.d: Drawing on DWF's 2019 prospectus, the authors describe its March 2019 IPO as a more comprehensive restructuring: a corporate parent raises external capital and supports multidisciplinary incentives while a partnership subsidiary retains advisory features. Partners receive a smaller partnership-profit component plus parent-company stock, and control rests with the corporate parent. This is an organizational example, not evidence that the structure ultimately outperforms alternatives.
qs: This type of structure has been adopted by DWF, a UK firm, which undertook an initial public offering in March 2019
The corporate parent (DWF Group plc) issued shares to outside investors in order to raise capital for investment, including in technology R&D.
At the same time, DWF seeks to retain many features of the legal advisory model by continuing to structure its law firm subsidiary as a partnership.

kp.k: Ownership regulation shapes available competitive strategies
kp.d: In its 2019–2020 account, the paper contrasts US restrictions associated with ABA Model Rule 5.4 and state adoption with the Legal Services Act 2007 regime in England and Wales. It describes contracting and law-firm-owned subsidiaries as available under restrictive rules, but non-lawyer partnerships and corporate parents as restricted. The authors argue that relaxed ownership rules enable external capital for R&D and market-share growth, potentially disadvantaging firms unable to use those structures.
qs: What remains restricted are partnerships with non-lawyers, or a move by a law firm to become a subsidiary of a public company.
the Legal Services Act 2007, which made it possible for legal advice to be offered by firms that are wholly or partly owned by non-lawyers
Such capital could be used not only to invest in R&D, but also to subsidize growth in market share and thereby stimulate data access.

kp.k: Hybrid professional roles challenge training and jurisdictional boundaries
kp.d: The authors predict more collaboration between lawyers and other experts, whether through separate specialists or individuals combining disciplines. Lawyers may increasingly design and manage services, including junior professionals incorporating technical and managerial expertise. Whether legal knowledge within these teams requires full lawyer qualification remains a contested issue involving efficiency, regulation and ethics. They predict stronger hybridization pressure under vertical integration than contracting.
qs: lawyers may come to design and manage the provision of good quality legal services, not just to give legal advice.
it embraces even junior professionals adopting managerial and technical expertise into their own professional practices and identities.
What is clear from our analysis is that the ‘legal’ bits in the multidisciplinary teams delivering new business models will need to become ‘hybridized’, and they need not even be lawyers.

lawyers working in law firms that access new business models by contracting face pressure to become hybridized to a lesser degree than lawyers working in organizations that access them via vertical integration.

kp.k: Advisory survival does not guarantee capturing AI-created value
kp.d: The authors reject a simple disappearance-of-lawyers narrative. They predict continuing demand for bespoke advisory work, while advisory-only firms increasingly consume technology and outsourced delivery and capture little AI-created value. Corporate clients, new entrants and diversified incumbents may share that value, potentially through consolidation. Which combinations of business models and governance structures will prove viable remains unresolved.
qs: Firms that focus exclusively on the legal advisory business model may therefore increasingly become consumers of legal technology products and legal operations services, but the logic of their business model will mean that they capture little of the value that is created by AI’s application.
Consolidation may mean they are combinations of the two.
The jury remains out on what are the viable business model combinations and governance forms for legal service providers.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Armour and Sako predict selective task substitution, continued human legal work, and the creation of new multidisciplinary tasks—not wholesale replacement of lawyers.
pts.d: The authors distinguish automating tasks from eliminating jobs. In their six-step AI workflow, generating outputs is automated, reducing the need for junior associates and paralegals doing document review. Defining problems, selecting and testing models, preparing data, reviewing outputs for consistency, and evaluating and explaining implications still require human inputs. These include legal expertise alongside data science, software engineering, information security, project management and design. Client-facing work and genuinely novel, bespoke legal solutions remain human comparative advantages under the capabilities described in the paper.

pts.k: AI's principal production advantage is scaling repeatable legal work, but data requirements and high fixed costs favour corporate legal services and well-resourced adopters.
pts.d: Armour and Sako argue that an operational ML system can generate predictions more cheaply, and often more accurately, than humans. They identify potential increasing returns when accuracy attracts users and additional use improves accuracy. However, training requires sufficiently large, representative datasets and expensive expert labelling. They infer that large commercial firms, corporate clients and externally funded entrants will lead adoption, rather than consumer legal services. This is a claim about enterprise adoption economics, not a finding about access to justice.

pts.k: AI enables three business-model opportunities with different pricing and value-capture mechanisms: process delivery, legal technology and consulting.
pts.d: The authors call the process-delivery model 'legal operations', explicitly applying that business-model label to both internal corporate provision and external service delivery. It lowers costs through workflow redesign and automation and can use fixed or per-unit fees, with AI-assisted price prediction helping make those fees possible. The legal technology model sells or licenses systems, including through subscriptions or software as a service, and captures value through intellectual property and platforms. Consulting designs and optimizes the combination of technology, processes and people; because it is bespoke and human-intensive, it can retain hourly pricing. Thus the paper does not predict that AI universally ends the billable hour. It also does not treat software vendors as interchangeable with ALSPs delivering legal work.

pts.k: The corporate form is a better organizational complement to legal operations and legal technology than the traditional professional partnership.
pts.d: Armour and Sako link AI-enabled delivery to technological assets, multidisciplinary teams, upfront risk investment and centralized coordination. They argue that corporations facilitate external equity funding, longer investment horizons and stock-based incentives for varied specialists. Conversely, lawyer ownership, partner consensus, lawyer-focused promotion and short investment horizons create internal obstacles in partnerships. The authors retain a role for partnerships in bespoke legal advisory work and explicitly qualify the comparison for consulting, whose human-capital intensity and hourly billing resemble traditional professional services. They also acknowledge that the Big Four's multidisciplinary partnerships differ from conventional law-firm partnerships.

pts.k: Corporate clients can capture AI benefits internally, but investment incentives and fragmented or insufficient data leave opportunities for external providers.
pts.d: The authors identify corporate clients' hierarchical management, multidisciplinary staffing and financing capacity as favourable starting points. Nevertheless, legal departments are usually treated as cost centres, making investments harder to justify than revenue-generating projects. Internal data can be scattered across legacy systems, and only very large clients may have enough matters to justify model training and labelling costs. External providers may achieve greater scale across clients, conditional on permission to share data. The resulting prediction is shared value capture, not complete insourcing or complete outsourcing.

pts.k: Different entrants have different advantages in exploiting AI-enabled legal business models.
pts.d: Armour and Sako describe technology startups as able to assemble specialized multidisciplinary teams and raise venture capital but constrained by reputation and access to users' training data. Established data providers such as LexisNexis and Thomson Reuters have an advantage in scaling AI based on their existing datasets. Law companies such as UnitedLex, Elevate and Axiom are described as expanding process-delivery capabilities and combining them with technology. The Big Four are positioned to combine the three new models and offer integrated legal and non-legal services. These are the paper's descriptions of the marketplace around 2019, not current company-status claims.

pts.k: Law-firm contracting offers a lower-commitment route into AI but can expose firms to client bypass, platform dependency and reduced value capture.
pts.d: The authors describe contracting with technology vendors or legal-service providers, and operating incubators, as ways to experiment without building complete multidisciplinary teams or raising external capital. They predict potential medium-term instability where suppliers also sell directly to corporate clients. Provider-specific training can create dependency and opportunities for renegotiation of the surplus. Pooling training benefits across customers could strengthen provider market power. Equity stakes and joint ventures are presented as means of reducing these adjustment and hold-up problems.

pts.k: Organizational separation and vertical integration can accommodate conflicting business models, but their long-term configuration remains unresolved.
pts.d: Armour and Sako argue that distinct operating units or corporate subsidiaries can preserve different staffing, incentives and governance arrangements rather than force technology and process businesses into the legal advisory partnership. Parent-funded subsidiaries still lack independent access to external capital. Scale incentives could eventually favour serving outside clients and spinning out; alternatively, continued integration could reform the parent firm. A corporate parent owning a law-firm partnership can support external investment and multidisciplinary incentives, illustrated by DWF's March 2019 IPO. The authors do not establish one universally superior structure.

pts.k: Ownership and fee-sharing regulation condition which organizational responses incumbents can pursue and may affect their competitiveness.
pts.d: The paper contrasts restrictions associated with ABA Model Rule 5.4 and state adoption of such restrictions with the nonlawyer-ownership opportunities created by the Legal Services Act 2007 in England and Wales. Under the restrictive regime described, law firms can contract with providers and own provider subsidiaries but cannot become subsidiaries of nonlawyer-owned public companies. The authors argue that access to corporate ownership can finance technology development and subsidize market-share growth that expands data access. They suggest that restrictions could disadvantage incumbents and generate reform pressure, identifying California in the contemporaneous discussion. This is a jurisdiction- and period-specific argument, not a statement that the ABA Model Rules themselves uniformly govern all US states.

pts.k: AI may divide legal careers between traditional advice and multidisciplinary delivery, with stronger hybridization pressures in integrated organizations.
pts.d: The authors predict that lawyers in AI-enabled businesses will increasingly design, organize and manage legal delivery alongside other specialists, including at junior levels. Whether the legal expertise in such teams must be supplied by fully qualified lawyers becomes a contested professional boundary shaped by efficiency pressures, regulation and ethics. Lawyers collaborating through contracts face less pressure to become hybrid professionals than those inside vertically integrated businesses. Meanwhile, firms retaining pure legal advisory models may survive and use AI-derived inputs while capturing little of the value generated by the technology.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The claims rest principally on a theoretical framework, existing scholarship and illustrative market developments, rather than original quantified tests of AI's effects.
pts.d: Armour and Sako explicitly build an account of complementarities across tasks, business models, assets and governance. Technical and task claims draw on machine-learning and labour-economics literature, including Autor, Brynjolfsson and Mitchell, Jurafsky and Martin, and Wooldridge. Adoption claims cite ABA TECHREPORT 2019 and the Legal Services Board's 2018 survey; entrant descriptions draw on the Thomson Reuters 2019 ALSP report, company materials and trade reporting. Illustrations include corporate legal-team reorganizations at GE, Barclays and BT; law-firm incubators and technology investments; EY's Riverview Law and Pangea3 acquisitions; and DWF's prospectus. These examples show reported experimentation, rather than a comparative demonstration of which structure performs best. The supplied paper reports no original model benchmark, measured cost-saving percentage, employment-effect estimate or causal test of organizational superiority. Its claim that predictions are often more accurate than human decisions is not accompanied by a specific legal-task benchmark.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The analysis describes the late-2019 adoption environment and offers conditional forecasts without a dated endpoint for market transformation.
pts.d: The supplied manuscript is dated December 2019 and identified as published in 2020. Its account of 'today's AI' primarily concerns supervised machine learning and NLP with large labelled-data requirements, rather than later general-purpose generative systems. Limits on social and creative intelligence are framed as holding for the foreseeable future, not permanently. Scaling depends on representative data, expert labelling, repeatable outputs, sufficient volume, multidisciplinary implementation and appropriate organizational complements. Provider market power depends partly on permission to pool data-derived training benefits. Corporate restructuring depends on jurisdictional ownership rules. Contractual instability is described as a medium-term possibility; subsidiary spinouts, consolidation and professional boundary changes have no fixed horizon.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The main affected groups are commercial legal providers, corporate buyers and the lawyers and other specialists working across their delivery systems.
pts.d: Junior associates and paralegals face reduced demand for repetitive output-generation tasks, while lawyers retain client-facing, bespoke, oversight and interpretive roles. Technical and managerial specialists become central contributors, creating demands for recognition, incentives and decision-making participation. Partners face challenges to consensus governance, exclusive profit sharing and traditional promotion arrangements. Large firms can experiment with contracting and corporate structures; smaller firms are described as largely remaining in advisory work. Corporate legal departments can capture savings but face investment and data constraints. ALSPs delivering work, legal-tech vendors selling systems, established data owners and the Big Four have distinct opportunities to capture value. The paper foregrounds corporate markets; it supplies no quantified forecast of total lawyer employment, consumer prices or changes in unmet civil legal need.
